                               PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS
                                      PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                                  SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                       JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY
                       COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION SERVICES
                        CORPORATION TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF
                      CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY
                         EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION 765-KV
                                TRANSMISSION LINE PROJECT

          JOHN BURROW'S REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES AND PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF
TEXAS:

I, John Burrow, a pro se intervenor, respectfully files this Reply to the Exceptions of Oncor Electric Delivery
Company LLC (Oncor) and Lower Colorado River Authority (LCRA) Transmission Services Corporations
(Applicants) and Public Utility Commission, Texas (PUC) Staff. John Burrow asks the AJL’s to adopt his
additional finding of facts, additional conclusion of law, and requested actions. John Burrow ask the ALJ’s
provide a recommendation that the Commission adopt the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH)
Proposal for Decision (PFD) for denial of the Application. John Burrow supports the reply and arguments
of Kevin Kennedy to the extent consistent with this filing. As such, John Burrow, will not reinvent the wheel
by repeating specific details brought to the attention of the ALJ’s by Kevin Kennedy in his exception reply.
John Burrow hopes to bolster the ALJ’s initial findings of facts, conclusion of law, and recommendation of
application denial.

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Oncor and PUC Staff's exceptions do not cure the defects the ALJs found. They largely ask the ALJ’s and
Commission to replace the evidentiary record with institutional deference, historical practice, and
assumptions. That is not enough for a multibillion-dollar 765-kV project that would impose permanent
easements across hundreds of miles of Texas.
First, Applicants' claim of public-meeting "precedent" is not precedent for what occurred here. Docket
59475 is materially different in both scale and effect. After the June 2025 public meetings, Applicants
expanded the study area and added roughly 400 plus miles of route links, bringing approximately 1,400
additional landowners into the filed routing universe without the public meeting opportunity given to the
original notified group of landowners. The earlier dockets cited by Applicants involved comparatively limited
modifications, modifications prompted by and responsive to participants already in the process, follow-up
notice to newly affected owners, or modifications agreed to by affected landowners. None establishes a
rule that a utility may radically expand a routing universe after its public meetings and exclude more than
25, much less approximately 1,400, newly affected landowners from the pre-filing participation process.
Second, the tax-roll issue is not an abstract dispute over whether "current" means the exact second an
application is filed. The record contains concrete evidence that Applicants mailed notice using ownership
information that was stale by many months, including property that had been subdivided long before filing
and lots sold as far back as December 2024. Applicants cannot convert proof of stale data into a semantic
argument over the word "current."
Third, the need case remains unproven. The PBRP recommendation is evidence, but it does not relieve
Applicants of their burden under PURA § 37.056 to prove that this specific Import Path 2 is necessary on
the record in this CCN case. The PFD found no independent partial-build study for Import Path 2, no
demonstrated source side, Bell County, generation position sufficient to support the claimed westbound
electricity transfer, no study showing Central Texas can simultaneously serve its growing local load and
export at the asserted level, and no proof that Import Path 2 is needed in 2030.

                              John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   1
 The need problem is deeper than changed forecasts. In Kevin Kennedy’s exceptions and reply of
exceptions shows the PBRP and the 2024 RTP were developed concurrently using materially different
load models. The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP, selectively added new Permian Transmission Service
Provider (TSP) loads, and modeled roughly 17 GW of planned generation; the contemporaneous 2024
RTP incorporated a much larger statewide load forecast and more than 59 GW of planned generation. If
the purpose is to determine long-distance import requirements, the load conditions in the supposed source
regions matter just as much as the load in the Permian sink. A model that updates the sink while leaving
materially older and lower load assumptions in the source regions can create an artificial source surplus
and overstate east-to-west transfer need. At minimum, that unresolved modeling prevents the PBRP from
carrying the dispositive weight Applicants and PUC Staff demand.
Fourth, we know what we are bringing forward and what we are talking about. Pro se intervenors, Kevin
Kennedy, retired Professional Engineer, former owner of a Engineering and Consulting Firm and John
Burrow, retired Civil Engineer, former Chief of Engineering for the Directorate of Public Works, Fort Hood
Garrison, Texas; find it ludicrous when the Applicants repeatedly attempt to diminish the landowner and
landowner evidence by labeling pro se intervenors as "lay persons" without transmission planning
expertise. This argument is fundamentally inconsistent with the process SOAH required these landowners
to follow. Intervenors were required to participate, conduct discovery, file testimony or statements of
position, identify exhibits, present evidence, withstand cross-examination, and brief the issues or risk
dismissal from the proceeding. Applicants cannot demand that landowners produce evidence and then
ask the ALJ’s and the Commission to disregard that evidence merely because those same landowners are
not utility employees, paid consultants, or professional expert witnesses.
The proper question is not who signed the paycheck or what title appears after a name. The proper
questions are whether the evidence is admitted, relevant, credible, supported by the record, and
persuasive. In this case, pro se intervenors did far more than offer unsupported opinions. They identified
missed landowners, stale ownership records, omitted homes and other features, post-meeting route
expansion, inconsistencies in load forecasts, gaps in generation assumptions, and differences between
the PBRP and later ERCOT planning models. In several instances, their work forced Applicants' own
records and assumptions into the light. Kevin Kennedy's tax-roll analysis, for example, relies on Applicants'
own discovery responses and demonstrates that ownership information used for notice was materially
stale.
A pro se landowner does not become less credible merely because he or she uncovered a problem that a
utility's consultants failed to identify. Nor may Applicants have it both ways: they cannot insist that
intervenors carry the burden of developing a factual record and then dismiss the resulting evidence as "lay
testimony" whenever it challenges Applicants' conclusions. The ALJs heard the witnesses, reviewed the
exhibits, weighed the competing evidence, and found significant portions of the intervenors' evidence
persuasive. The ALJ’s and the Commission should evaluate that evidence on its merits, not based on the
professional status of the person who brought it forward. To do otherwise would reduce public participation
to an empty formality: landowners would be required to prove their case, but their proof would be
discounted simply because they were forced to represent themselves.
The fact that ordinary landowners were able to uncover material notice and modeling problems after
Applicants had the benefit of engineers, lawyers, consultants, and months of preparation strengthens the
significance of that evidence; it does not diminish it.
Lastly, the Commission final ruling on Docket 59315 also raise a more fundamental question concerning
the integrity of the contested case process. The purpose of referring these proceedings to SOAH and
conducting a full hearing on the merits is to develop an evidentiary record before neutral ALJs who hear
the testimony, evaluate the evidence, consider the arguments of all parties, and make findings and
recommendations based upon that record. Here, on Docket 59475, after an extensive contested-case
proceeding, the ALJs concluded that significant deficiencies existed concerning public-meeting notice,
the use of current tax records, and the Applicants ’proof of need, and ultimately recommended denial of
the Application. While the Commission retains final decision-making authority, the SOAH process should
have substantive meaning. If findings reached after a full evidentiary hearing can be displaced merely
because an applicant or another party disagrees with the result, without identifying substantial record
                             John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   2
 evidence or a controlling legal error requiring a different conclusion, it raises the question of what
meaningful purpose the hearing on the merits served. The Commission should give substantial
consideration (Great Weight) to the ALJ’s findings precisely because those findings resulted from the
evidentiary process established to test the Applicants ’claims, protect the rights of affected landowners,
and create a reliable record for the Commission’s final decision. The Commission should not substitute a
preferred outcome for findings reached through that process absent a sound legal and record-based
basis for doing so.
This concern is particularly important because the Commission’s final order must ultimately stand on the
administrative record. The ALJs did not reach their recommendation in a vacuum. Their findings followed
discovery, pre-filed testimony, exhibits, cross-examination, a hearing on the merits, and post-hearing
briefing in which the Applicants had a full opportunity to meet their burden of proof. If the Commission
rejects material findings or conclusions of the ALJs, particularly findings that contributed to the
recommended denial of the Application, the basis for doing so should be clearly identified and supported
by the evidentiary record and applicable law. Otherwise, the contested-case process risks becoming little
more than a procedural exercise in which affected landowners are required to expend substantial time
and resources developing evidence and participating in a hearing, only to have record-based findings
displaced without an adequate explanation. Such an outcome would not only undermine confidence in
the SOAH process but could also raise substantial questions on judicial review concerning whether the
Commission’s ultimate findings and conclusions are reasonably supported by substantial evidence and
whether the agency adequately explained its departure from the evidentiary findings developed through
the contested-case process. John Burrow therefore respectfully urges the PUC and SOAH to preserve
the integrity of this process.

The ALJ’s should maintain their recommendation of denial based on the evidence presented and
Commission should adopt the PFD's denial recommendation. The exceptions do not demonstrate that
the ALJs misapplied the law or that their material findings lack support in the record.

II. THE PUBLIC-MEETING EXCEPTIONS SHOULD BE REJECTED
A. Applicants and PUC Staff confuse ordinary route refinement with a wholesale expansion of the
affected public.
Applicants characterize the issue as whether a utility may ever add or modify a link after a public meeting.
That is not the issue the PFD decided. The PFD addressed an extraordinary factual record: three meetings
were held in June 2025; thereafter the study area was expanded and roughly 400 miles of links were
added; and approximately 1,400 later-affected landowners became persons entitled to application notice
without ever receiving the pre-filing public-meeting opportunity afforded to the earlier group.
Rule 22.52(a)(4) ties the meeting requirement to the number of persons who "would be entitled to receive
direct mail notice of the application." The PFD reasonably applied that language to the filed routing
universe. Applicants controlled when they filed. Once their post-meeting redesign created a new class far
exceeding the 25-person trigger, they could have held an additional meeting before filing. The evidence
shows in Requests for Information (RFI), the Applicants were aware of and internally discussed the
possibility of an additional public meeting five to six months before filing. They knew, they discussed it,
they control timing of an application notice, and they chose not to hold one.
Application notice after the routes have been developed is not a substitute for public-meeting notice before
filing. The two notices serve different functions. A public meeting is designed to obtain community values,
local constraints, and routing information while alternatives are still being developed. Application notice
tells a landowner that the utility has already selected the universe of routes to litigate and that a contested
case has begun. Treating the latter as a cure for the former erases the participation right created by
subsection (a)(4).




                              John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   3
 B. The cited dockets do not establish a controlling Commission precedent for Docket 59475.
Applicants' exceptions repeatedly use the word "precedent," but the cited orders do not decide the factual
and legal question presented here: whether, after public meetings, an applicant may add hundreds of miles
of new route links that newly affect approximately 1,400 landowners and still claim that the original
meetings satisfied the rule for those newly affected owners. The ALJ’s should not accept this claim, and
the Commission should compare what actually happened in the cited cases, not merely the fact that some
route changed after a meeting.

 Magnitude Comparison


The mileage comparison is the central factual distinction. Using approximately 353 miles of entirely new
routing in Docket 59475 as the common comparison point, the post-meeting new routing was
approximately:
 • 254 times the mileage identified in Docket 51023 (approx. 1.39 miles);
 • 79 times the mileage identified in Docket 49523 after its final meeting (approx. 4.48 miles);
 • 68 times the mileage identified in Docket 48358 (approx. 5.2 miles);
 • 65 times the mileage identified in Docket 45624 (approx. 5.47 miles); and
 • nearly 16 times the mileage identified in Docket 51912 (approx. 22.36 miles).


This comparison shows by adding 400 plus miles of routes, links, and segments, you have created a large
project modification, new scope, and essentially a new project. The most important point is not whether
prior utilities ever changed routes. Of course they did. The question is whether those cases authorized
what happened here. They did not. Applicants have identified no Commission order holding that a utility
may add approximately 400 miles of routes, expand the study area, newly affect approximately 1,400
landowners, and deny that entire new class the pre-filing public-meeting opportunity while still satisfying
Rule 22.52(a)(4).
The Commission's treatment of Docket 59315 does not establish a controlling rule for this case and
reinforces why the Commission should examine the facts of each prior docket before treating them as
precedent. The ALJ’s and Commission should also reject the argument that enforcing the rule here creates
an endless cycle of meetings. The rule already supplies an objective trigger: 25 or more persons entitled
to application notice. The PFD does not require a meeting for every minor adjustment. It addresses a case
where the post-meeting expansion itself created a massive new affected population. A utility can refine
routes without restarting the process for trivial changes; it cannot use the phrase "preliminary routes" as a
blank check to redesign a project on this scale after the public has been divided into two unequal classes.
C. The prejudice was substantive, not technical.
The original notified landowners had months to attend meetings, speak with routing personnel, identify
homes, schools, churches, development, and other constraints, and influence route development before
filing. The later added landowners did not. They entered only after the route universe had been
substantially developed and then faced a compressed 30-day intervention deadline and a 180-day
statutory case schedule. The PFD correctly recognized that this asymmetry cannot be dismissed as
harmless merely because some later owners managed to intervene.
The fact that some late-noticed landowners fought their way into the case does not prove the process
worked; it proves that they had to overcome a defect that the earlier group did not face.

III. THE CURRENT-TAX-ROLL EXCEPTIONS SHOULD BE REJECTED
A. PUC Staff's grammatical argument cannot overcome the evidence of stale ownership data.
PUC Staff argues that the phrase "on the date it files an application" modifies "mail" rather than "current
county tax rolls," and therefore the rule does not require a same day pull of tax data. That argument attacks
a straw man. The PFD's core factual point is not that every record had to be downloaded at 12:01 a.m. on
March 26, 2026. It is that Applicants bore the burden to use current county tax-roll information and the
evidence showed that they did not.
The record identified in Kevin Kennedy's reply is concrete. Bell County Appraisal District advised that its
mapping is updated continuously. Yet Applicants' March 26 application still treated Tract 3276 as a single
parcel owned by BWH Holdings LLC-Series 2 even though the tract had been subdivided into roughly 25
residential lots in September 2024. Applicants later discovered that lots had been sold long before filing,
including sales dating to December 12, 2024, and that subsequent purchasers owned the properties by

                             John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   6
 the filing date. Applicants' own later corrections are evidence that the mailing data used on March 26 was
not current.
If data can be 12 to 15 months behind recorded subdivisions and ownership transfers and still be called
"current," then the word becomes meaningless. The Commission should not interpret its rule in a manner
that reads an express protection out of the text.
B. Administrative convenience cannot rewrite a notice rule.
PUC Staff emphasizes the burden of preparing thousands of lengthy notice packets across fifteen counties.
The magnitude of Applicants' project is not a legal exemption. The larger the project and the greater the
eminent-domain consequences, the more important accurate ownership data becomes. Applicants
selected the filing date and controlled their notice-preparation process. Reasonable lead time may be
necessary; year-old ownership information is a different matter.
Nor does later actual participation cure the initial failure. Rule 22.52(a)(3) protects the class of directly
affected landowners, not merely those who independently discover the case in time. A process that misses
owners and then points to the subset who eventually intervened cannot establish compliance by a
preponderance of the evidence.

IV. APPLICANTS AND PUC STAFF STILL HAVE NOT PROVED NEED
A. "Great weight" is not conclusive weight and does not shift the statutory burden.
PUC Staff's need exception is built around deference: ERCOT recommended the PBRP, the Commission
approved Import Path 1, and later planning studies assumed the 765-kV import paths. But the legal
question in this docket is whether Applicants proved that Import Path 2 is necessary under PURA § 37.056.
Great weight to ERCOT is not a presumption that converts a planning recommendation into an irrebuttable
adjudicative fact.
The PFD identified record-specific deficiencies that deference cannot cure: Applicants did not perform a
partial build study establishing independent need for Import Path 2; ERCOT's sequencing indicated only
two of the three paths were needed for 2030 load; Applicants did not establish the net generation position
in Central Texas; no determination was made that Central Texas could serve local data-center growth
while simultaneously exporting westward at the claimed capability; and no analysis tested project viability
if the assumed Central Texas generation surplus did not exist.
Those are not policy disagreements. They are missing engineering proof. A transmission path designed to
move bulk power from one region to another cannot be shown necessary merely by assuming the source
region has power available to export.
B. Later RTPs cannot bootstrap the PBRP when those RTPs assumed the import paths were
already in service.
Applicants and PUC Staff point to the 2024 and 2025 RTPs as confirmation. But Applicants' own exception
states that those systemwide models assume the Import Path projects are in service. A study that assumes
the disputed facilities exist and then demonstrates power flows through a network containing those facilities
does not independently prove that the facilities were necessary in the first place. That is circular.
This is especially important because the later RTPs also identify substantial Central Texas load growth
and import requirements. Those results raise the opposite question: if Central Texas is itself becoming a
load sink, what verified surplus is available at Bell County East to support the long-haul westbound transfer
claimed for Import Path 2? The PFD correctly refused to fill that evidentiary gap with assumptions.
C. The PBRP modeling asymmetry goes to the reliability of the very evidence on which
Applicants rely.
Kevin Kennedy's reply identifies a serious modeling issue already grounded in record exhibits: the PBRP
and 2024 RTP were developed during the same period but from materially different load-model vintages.
The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP and selectively incorporated new TSP provided Permian loads. The
contemporaneous 2024 RTP incorporated the much larger statewide TSP load forecast.

                             John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   7
 The numerical contrast is substantial. The PBRP modeled approximately 17,170 MW of planned
generation. The 2024 RTP used approximately 59,202 MW of future planned generation to balance the
broader statewide load assumptions a difference of roughly 42,000 MW. The PBRP itself acknowledged
approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand across ERCOT by 2030 outside the narrow Permian
focus. Yet the PBRP import analysis did not model that statewide future load on the same basis used for
its concentrated Permian load additions.
That matters because power flow follows the geographic relationship between generation and load. If the
Permian sink is updated with very large new loads while potential source regions retain older and lower
load assumptions, and future generation is added elsewhere to balance the case, the model can create
an artificial central Texas surplus and therefore an exaggerated east to west transfer requirement. This is
not an accusation that a computer produced the wrong arithmetic. It is a challenge to the assumptions fed
into the model, and assumptions determine results.
Applicants call the PBRP the foundation of need. If the foundation uses an asymmetric load picture, the
ALJ’s and the Commission cannot simply give the resulting recommendation "great weight" and stop
asking questions. Before condemning private property for a $4 to $5-billion import path, the Commission
should require a statewide reliability model that places the known future TSP load and generation
assumptions on a consistent temporal and geographic basis and then tests whether any Import Path
remains independently necessary.
D. PURA § 37.056(c-1) makes forecasted load a statutory input, not an optional modeling choice.
PURA § 37.056(c-1), as amended in the HB 5066 framework, requires consideration of historical load,
forecasted load growth, and additional load seeking interconnection, including load without a signed
interconnection agreement as determined by the responsible utility. Kennedy's exception argues that the
PBRP did not include approximately 42,000 MW of known future TSP load outside the Permian that was
reflected in the contemporaneous statewide planning process.
Applicants cannot have it both ways. They rely on HB 5066 as legislative validation of the PBRP, while
resisting scrutiny of whether the model used the statewide load information the statute required the
Commission to consider. If the record shows materially different treatment of known TSP load depending
on geography, the appropriate response is not more deference. It is to require a consistent statewide
analysis before finding need.
E. Changed circumstances independently weaken the original PBRP forecast.
Even apart from the modeling asymmetry, the PFD found material changes since the PBRP: ERCOT
adopted a realization-rate methodology that would materially reduce non-oil-and-gas load; the record
showed a reduction of at least 3,571 MW under the updated methodology; a large share of the PBRP non-
oil-and-gas forecast was cryptocurrency mining load; and the oil-and-gas forecast relied on an older S&P
Global study the ALJs found overstated and outdated. Senate Bill 6 and Batch Zero further reflect the
State's concern that large-load requests may not all materialize.
PUC Staff's response is essentially that ERCOT has not changed its recommendation. But persistence of
a recommendation is not a substitute for re-running the critical assumptions. The question is whether the
recommendation remains supported after the forecast and modeling concerns are accounted for. The PFD
found that Applicants did not carry that burden.
F. The Commission should not approve a first-of-its-kind 765-kV import path on circular
assumptions.
Texas has never constructed a 765-kV transmission line. Import Path 2 alone is a roughly 400-plus-mile
two-project corridor with multibillion-dollar cost and enormous permanent land impacts. The Commission
does not need certainty about every future generator. It does need substantial evidence that the specific
project is necessary and can perform the reliability function asserted for it.
Here, the record did not establish independent 2030 need for Import Path 2, did not establish the source-
side generation surplus, did not test a partial build, did not test the Central Texas load growth that could


                             John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   8
 absorb the supposed export supply, and relied heavily on a PBRP model whose statewide load treatment
is directly challenged by record evidence. That is not enough to satisfy PURA § 37.056.

V. RESPONSE TO ROUTING EXCEPTIONS
John Burrow agrees with the PFD that the Application should be denied and that no routing decision should
be reached. Only in the alternative, if the Commission rejects the PFD's denial recommendation and
reaches routing, Burrow continues to oppose Route 894 and Route 487.

VI. SUPPORT FOR THE REPLY OF KEVIN KENNEDY
John Burrow supports Kevin Kennedy's record-based tax-roll analysis and his engineering challenge to
the PBRP's asymmetric load and generation assumptions. Kennedy's reply does not ask the Commission
to accept a new outside study; it asks the Commission to examine the PBRP and 2024 RTP exhibits
already in the record together and confront the materially different modeling inputs they reveal. John
Burrow relies on the underlying record evidence and requests findings stated in measured factual terms
rather than characterizing the PBRP as categorically invalid.

VII. PROPOSED ADDITIONAL FINDINGS OF FACT AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
In addition to adopting the PFD's existing findings and conclusions, John Burrow respectfully requests that
the Commission adopt the following additional findings and conclusions to address issues raised in the
exceptions and supported by the existing record.
A. Proposed Additional Findings of Fact - Public Meeting and Notice
1. Applicants mailed approximately 2,809 notices of the June 2025 public meetings but mailed more than
   approximately 4,200 notices of the Application filed March 26, 2026.
2. Applicants' post-public-meeting routing changes increased the affected landowner population by
   approximately 1,400 landowners.
3. Applicants internally considered whether to conduct an additional public meeting after the post-meeting
   expansion of the study area and routing alternatives but did not conduct an additional public meeting
   before filing the Application 6 months later.
4. The approximately 1,400 newly affected landowners did not receive the same pre-filing opportunity as
   the originally affected landowners to provide information concerning community values, residences,
   schools, churches, land use, routing constraints, and potential route modifications before the routing
   alternatives were finalized for filing.
B. Proposed Additional Findings of Fact - Current County Tax Rolls
5. Bell County Appraisal District advised Applicants' notice consultant that its mapping information is
   updated continuously throughout the year.
6. On March 26, 2026, Applicants' Application identified Tract 3276 as a single parcel owned by BWH
   Holdings LLC-Series 2.
7. Tract 3276 had been subdivided into approximately 25 residential lots in September 2024, approximately
   18 months before Applicants filed the Application.
8. Before the March 26, 2026, filing date, portions of the former Tract 3276 had been conveyed to other
   owners.
9. Applicants subsequently revised their ownership information after filing the Application to reflect the
   subdivision and ownership changes.
10. The ownership information used by Applicants for the March 26, 2026, notice therefore did not identify
   all directly affected owners reflected by more current ownership information available before the
   Application was filed March 26, 2026.


                             John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   9
 C. Proposed Additional Findings of Fact - Need and PBRP Modeling
11. ERCOT developed the PBRP and the 2024 RTP during overlapping planning periods using materially
   different load and generation assumptions.
12. The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP 2029 West/Far West model and incorporated additional TSP-
   provided Permian Basin load.
13. The PBRP itself acknowledged that TSP forecasts used in the 2024 RTP identified approximately
   59,400 MW of additional demand across the ERCOT system that would need to be served by 2030.
14. The PBRP modeled approximately 17,170 MW of planned generation, while the contemporaneous
   2024 RTP reflected approximately 59,202 MW of future planned generation.
15. Applicants did not demonstrate that the PBRP import-path analysis incorporated the contemporaneous
   statewide TSP load forecast on the same basis that it incorporated the additional Permian Basin load.
16. Applicants did not present a analysis testing whether Import Path 2 remains necessary when
   contemporaneous load growth in potential source regions, including Central Texas, is incorporated into
   the analysis.
17. Applicants did not perform an independent partial-build study establishing the need for Import Path 2
   individually.
18. Applicants did not establish Central Texas's net generation position under current conditions, projected
   2030 conditions, or projected conditions incorporating significant large-load growth.
19. Applicants did not establish that sufficient generation will be available in Central Texas to

If data can be 12 to 15 months behind recorded subdivisions and ownership transfers and still be called

PUC Staff emphasizes the burden of preparing thousands of lengthy notice packets across fifteen counties.

IV. APPLICANTS AND PUC STAFF STILL HAVE NOT PROVED NEED
A. "Great weight" is not conclusive weight and does not shift the statutory burden.
PUC Staffs need exception is built around deference: ERCOT recommended the PBRP, the Commission
approved Import Path 1, and later planning studies assumed the 765-kV import paths. But the legal
question in this docket is whether Applicants proved that Import Path 2 is necessary under PURA § 37.056.
Great weight to ERCOT is not a presumption that converts a planning recommendation into an irrebuttable
adjudicative fact.
The PFD identified record-specific deficiencies that deference cannot cure: Applicants did not perform a
partial build study establishing independent need for Import Path 2; ERCOT's sequencing indicated only
two of the three paths were needed for 2030 load; Applicants did not establish the net generation position
in Central Texas; no determination was made that Central Texas could serve local data-center growth
while simultaneously exporting westward at the claimed capability; and no analysis tested project viability
if the assumed Central Texas generation surplus did not exist.
Those are not policy disagreements. They are missing engineering proof. A transmission path designed to
move bulk power from one region to another cannot be shown necessary merely by assuming the source
region has power available to export.
B. Later RTPs cannot bootstrap the PBRP when those RTPs assumed the import paths were
already in service.
Applicants and PUC Staff point to the 2024 and 2025 RTPs as confirmation. But Applicants' own exception
states that those systemwide models assume the Import Path projects are in service. A study that assumes
the disputed facilities exist and then demonstrates power flows through a network containing those facilities
does not independently prove that the facilities were necessary in the first place. That is circular.
This is especially important because the later RTPs also identify substantial Central Texas load growth
and import requirements. Those results raise the opposite question: if Central Texas is itself becoming a
load sink, what verified surplus is available at Bell County East to support the long-haul westbound transfer
claimed for Import Path 2? The PFD correctly refused to fill that evidentiary gap with assumptions.
C. The PBRP modeling asymmetry goes to the reliability of the very evidence on which
Applicants rely.
Kevin Kennedy's reply identifies a serious modeling issue already grounded in record exhibits: the PBRP
and 2024 RTP were developed during the same period but from materially different load-model vintages.
The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP and selectively incorporated new TSP provided Permian loads. The
contemporaneous 2024 RTP incorporated the much larger statewide TSP load forecast.

                              John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   7
 The numerical contrast is substantial. The PBRP modeled approximately 17,170 MW of planned
generation. The 2024 RTP used approximately 59,202 MW of future planned generation to balance the
broader statewide load assumptions a difference of roughly 42,000 MW. The PBRP itself acknowledged
approximately 59,400 MW of additional demand across ERCOT by 2030 outside the narrow Permian
focus. Yet the PBRP import analysis did not model that statewide future load on the same basis used for
its concentrated Permian load additions.
That matters because power flow follows the geographic relationship between generation and load. If the
Permian sink is updated with very large new loads while potential source regions retain older and lower
load assumptions, and future generation is added elsewhere to balance the case, the model can create
an artificial central Texas surplus and therefore an exaggerated east to west transfer requirement. This is
not an accusation that a computer produced the wrong arithmetic. It is a challenge to the assumptions fed
into the model, and assumptions determine results.
Applicants call the PBRP the foundation of need. If the foundation uses an asymmetric load picture, the
ALJ's and the Commission cannot simply give the resulting recommendation "great weight" and stop
asking questions. Before condemning private property for a $4 to $5-billion import path, the Commission
should require a statewide reliability model that places the known future TSP load and generation
assumptions on a consistent temporal and geographic basis and then tests whether any Import Path
remains independently necessary.
D. PURA § 37.056(c-1) makes forecasted load a statutory input, not an optional modeling choice.
PURA § 37.056(c-1), as amended in the HB 5066 framework, requires consideration of historical load,
forecasted load growth, and additional load seeking interconnection, including load without a signed
interconnection agreement as determined by the responsible utility. Kennedy's exception argues that the
PBRP did not include approximately 42,000 MW of known future TSP load outside the Permian that was
reflected in the contemporaneous statewide planning process.
Applicants cannot have it both ways. They rely on HB 5066 as legislative validation of the PBRP, while
resisting scrutiny of whether the model used the statewide load information the statute required the
Commission to consider. If the record shows materially different treatment of known TSP load depending
on geography, the appropriate response is not more deference. It is to require a consistent statewide
analysis before finding need.
E. Changed circumstances independently weaken the original PBRP forecast.
Even apart from the modeling asymmetry, the PFD found material changes since the PBRP: ERCOT
adopted a realization-rate methodology that would materially reduce non-oil-and-gas load; the record
showed a reduction of at least 3,571 MW under the updated methodology; a large share of the PBRP non-
oil-and-gas forecast was cryptocurrency mining load; and the oil-and-gas forecast relied on an older S&P
Global study the ALJs found overstated and outdated. Senate Bill 6 and Batch Zero further reflect the
State's concern that large-load requests may not all materialize.
PUC Staffs response is essentially that ERCOT has not changed its recommendation. But persistence of
a recommendation is not a substitute for re-running the critical assumptions. The question is whether the
recommendation remains supported after the forecast and modeling concerns are accounted for. The PFD
found that Applicants did not carry that burden.
F. The Commission should not approve a first-of-its-kind 765-kV import path on circular
assumptions.
Texas has never constructed a 765-kV transmission line. Import Path 2 alone is a roughly 400-plus-mile
two-project corridor with multibillion-dollar cost and enormous permanent land impacts. The Commission
does not need certainty about every future generator. It does need substantial evidence that the specific
project is necessary and can perform the reliability function asserted for it.
Here, the record did not establish independent 2030 need for Import Path 2, did not establish the source-
side generation surplus, did not test a partial build, did not test the Central Texas load growth that could

                                John Burrow - Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision   8
 absorb the supposed export supply, and relied heavily on a PBRP model whose statewide load treatment
is directly challenged by record evidence. That is not enough to satisfy PURA § 37.056.

 C. Proposed Additional Findings of Fact - Need and PBRP Modeling
11. ERCOT developed the PBRP and the 2024 RTP during overlapping planning periods using materially
   different load and generation assumptions.
12. The PBRP began with the 2023 RTP 2029 West/Far West model and incorporated additional TSP-
   provided Permian Basin load.
13. The PBRP itself acknowledged that TSP forecasts used in the 2024 RTP identified approximately
   59,400 MW of additional demand across the ERCOT system that would need to be served by 2030.
14. The PBRP modeled approximately 17,170 MW of planned generation, while the contemporaneous
   2024 RTP reflected approximately 59,202 MW of future planned generation.
15. Applicants did not demonstrate that the PBRP import-path analysis incorporated the contemporaneous
   statewide TSP load forecast on the same basis that it incorporated the additional Permian Basin load.
16. Applicants did not present a analysis testing whether Import Path 2 remains necessary when
   contemporaneous load growth in potential source regions, including Central Texas, is incorporated into
  the analysis.
17. Applicants did not perform an independent partial-build study establishing the need for Import Path 2
   individually.
18. Applicants did not establish Central Texas's net generation position under current conditions, projected
  2030 conditions, or projected conditions incorporating significant large-load growth.
19. Applicants did not establish that sufficient generation will be available in Central Texas to
   simultaneously serve projected Central Texas load and provide the westbound transfer relied upon to
   justify Import Path 2.
20. ERCOT's sequencing analysis determined that two of the three 765-kV import paths were needed for
   forecasted 2030 Permian Basin load and prioritized the northern and southern import paths rather than
   Import Path 2.
21. The post-public-meeting routing expansion in Docket No. 59475 added approximately 353 miles of
   entirely new routing and approximately 68.3 miles of new portions of modified links, substantially
   exceeding the post-meeting additions identified in Dockets Nos. 45624, 49523, 51023, 48358, and
   51912.
D. Proposed Additional Conclusions of Law
1. The record does not establish by a preponderance of the evidence that Import Path 2 is independently
   necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public under PURA § 37.056.
2. The Commission's disposition of public-meeting issues in the prior proceedings cited by Applicants does
   not control the materially different factual circumstances presented in Docket No. 59475.
3. The material differences between the PBRP and contemporaneous statewide planning assumptions
   reduce the weight that can reasonably be afforded the PBRP as proof of independent need for Import
   Path 2 unless those differences are reconciled by record evidence.

IX. CONCLUSION
This case should not be decided by saying, in effect, "we have done something similar before" or "ERCOT
recommended it before." The Commission is deciding this record, this project, and these landowners. The
record shows a post-meeting routing expansion of extraordinary scale, approximately 1,400 newly affected
landowners denied the pre-filing meeting opportunity, stale ownership information used for legal notice,
and a need case that depends on assumptions Applicants never independently validated for Import Path
2.
The ALJs heard the evidence, weighed the competing testimony, and concluded that Applicants did not
comply with the notice rules and did not prove need. Applicants' and Staffs exceptions do not eliminate
those evidentiary failures. They ask the Commission to excuse them. The Commission should decline to
do so, adopt the requested additional findings and conclusions, and adopt the PFD's recommended denial.
